description_full: Franklin Templeton Inc. is a publicly owned asset investment manager. Through its subsidiaries, the firm provides its services to individuals, institutions, pension plans, trusts, and partnerships. It launches equity, fixed income, balanced, and multi-asset mutual funds through its subsidiaries. The firm invests in the public equity, fixed income, and alternative markets. Franklin Resources, Inc. was founded in 1947 and is based in San Mateo, California with an additional office in Calgary, Alberta; Dubai, United Arab Emirates; Edinburgh, Midlothian; Fort Lauderdale, Florida; Hyderabad, India; London, Greater London; Rancho Cordova, California; Shanghai, Shanghai Province; Singapore; Stamford, Connecticut; and Vienna.
ceo_bio: Ms. Jennifer M. Johnson | CEO & Non-Independent Director | Age 61 | Compensation: $7.9M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 10K people. Revenue per employee of $868K ranks in the above the sector median among Financial Services peers. Each employee generates $90K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $21K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 9× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (7/10).
financial_summary: Franklin Templeton, Inc. is a large-cap financial services business with a $17.1B market cap on $8.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years and +1% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 6% against a 10% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $912M in free cash flow — roughly 10 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.03× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.2× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 6.4×.

Management returns a meaningful 5.3% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 49% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and profit capture is only 0.3× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 7% operating margin trails the Financial Services median (29%) by 22pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.27x its revenue share).
It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 0.1% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-19.9% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.02 across 512 companies in the universe; the top four hold 20% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 46% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 7% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 28% and a beta of 1.12, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $113.4M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 42% in the 2020 crash, 39% in the 2022 bear market and 66% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $24.15 (margin of safety -40%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 21%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $16.18 to $35.79 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Financial Services peers: P/E 22.9 vs 12.2 and P/FCF 18.8 vs 12.9 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 306% above its 10-year median.
The 13 covering analysts target $35.46 on average, 5% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
The price implies 16.1% annual cash-flow growth, 4pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 6% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.5%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.58).
It converts 10% of revenue into free cash flow.
It earns a 4% return on equity.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 2.0% over 3 years, 9.5% over 5 years and 1.0% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 17%).
At current returns, reinvesting 7% of profits supports about 0.4% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 21.6% on average.
Analysts expect 12.7% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own 48.7%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 50%.
It returns 5.3% a year to shareholders (1.3% in buybacks and 3.9% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 40 consecutive years, raising it 5.1% a year over the last five.
people: With about 10,100 employees, each generates about $868K of revenue, 1.7x the Financial Services median, and productivity has risen 4.7% a year.
That works out to $90K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $7.9M (9x revenue per employee).
